To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability of Purkinjie cells to rapidly buffer calcium transients increases during development, that this increase is related to an increase in the total concentration of calcium binding proteins, and that this increase is not related to an increase of calcium current.

(i) the calcium binding ratio of Purkyne cells is 10 fold greater than that of any other cell type studied to date, (ii) this ratio decreases by approximately 50 % during the first postnatal week, and (iii) this decrease is not associated with a reduction in the calcium currents that are responsible for calcium loading of these cells.

Purkinje cells are able to buffer Ca2+ loads 2000 times more effectively than other neurones, and that they do this through the presence of large amounts of Ca2+ buffers, which they regulate during development.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the cerebellar cortex.
the development of a new method to estimate the ability of neurones to buffer changes in intracellular calcium concentration.
the mechanisms that regulate intracellular calcium in neurons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the large Ca(2+) binding ratio of Purkyne cells is due to a large concentration of Ca2+-binding proteins and the cells regulate their ability for handling Ca2+ loads through development through changes in concentration of Ca2-binding proteins.
the Ca2+ buffer capacity of Purkinje neurones is very high, and that the Ca2+/calmodulin‐dependent protein kinase II (CaMK II) may be the main Ca2+ buffer.
Purkinje cells have a large Ca2+ buffer capacity.

Purkinje cells can buffer Ca2+ loads by a factor of 10,000.
the Purkinje cell is an excellent example of the ability of cells to adjust their Ca2+ handling properties to their particular requirements.

the Purkinje cells are able to buffer the calcium loads by binding them to proteins.
the large Ca(2+) binding ratios observed in Purkinje neurones are due to the presence of high levels of Ca(2+) buffers.
